title: Medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding
blurb: Recognise key teratogens (valproate, ACE inhibitors, lithium), support safe antihypertensive use with breastfeeding, and use reliable information sources.
question: Funmi, of Black African family origin, has postnatal hypertension and is breastfeeding her 4-day-old baby. She worries her tablets will harm the baby. What should the midwife advise?

teach.body: Formally, a teratogen is a substance that can disrupt the development of an embryo or fetus, causing birth defects, developmental delay, miscarriage, stillbirth or growth restriction. In plain English: some medicines can harm a baby before birth, so they are avoided or switched before or early in pregnancy. After birth the picture changes: most medicines can be used during breastfeeding, and stopping breastfeeding is not a risk-free option for mother or baby (SPS).
teach.cite: SPS: risks and principles of prescribing in pregnancy (2025); advising on medicines during breastfeeding (2026)

teach.h: Breastfeeding is compatible with most treatment
teach.body: NICE says antihypertensives do not prevent breastfeeding: most give very low levels in milk, and warnings in the manufacturer's leaflet usually reflect lack of testing, not evidence of harm (NG133 1.9.1-1.9.2). Advise parents to watch the baby for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries or poor feeding (1.9.3). SPS adds: monitoring matters most for young, preterm or exclusively breastfed babies; codeine should not be used when breastfeeding; lithium can reach high levels in milk (CG192 1.4.34).

teach.caption: Seek expert advice if in doubt, and before ever advising a woman to stop breastfeeding (SPS).

teach.body: Funmi can keep breastfeeding: NICE says her treatment can be adapted to breastfeeding and the amounts reaching the baby are very small. Because she is of Black African family origin, NICE suggests nifedipine (or amlodipine if it worked for her before) rather than enalapril first. The midwife explains what to watch for in the baby (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold hands and feet, poor feeding), checks feeding and nappies, and makes sure the plan is on her discharge summary.

teach.text: Do not carry pregnancy rules into the postnatal period blindly. ACE inhibitors are stopped in pregnancy, yet enalapril is NICE's first-choice antihypertensive after birth, including when breastfeeding. And do not tell a woman to stop valproate herself: urgent specialist advice comes first.

items: Valproate: about 1 in 9 birth defects and 3-4 in 10 developmental problems; PPP; urgent specialist review.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs: stop within 2 working days of pregnancy notification and switch.
Lithium: heart malformation risk in the first trimester; high levels in breast milk.
Postnatal BP when breastfeeding: enalapril; nifedipine or amlodipine for Black African or Caribbean women; avoid diuretics and ARBs.
Sources: UKTIS and BUMPS for pregnancy, SPS and UKDILAS for breastfeeding, BNF and SPC.

summary: You can now recognise the main teratogens a midwife meets and escalate them promptly, support women to continue breastfeeding while taking antihypertensives, and choose reliable sources of advice. You can also tell parents what to watch for in a breastfed baby.

A.q: Jade asks how likely valproate is to cause a birth defect if taken in pregnancy. What does MHRA guidance say?
options: No extra risk with folic acid
A.why: MHRA (2025): in women who take valproate while pregnant, around 1 in 9 babies (11%) will have a birth defect, and 3 or 4 in 10 children may have developmental problems.

whyNot.1: 1 in 2 overstates the birth defect risk.
whyNot.3: Folic acid does not remove the valproate risk.

A.q: Rachel takes ramipril for chronic hypertension and has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. What should the midwife ensure?
options: She continues it until the 12-week scan
The prescriber stops and switches it promptly
All of her BP treatment is stopped
She continues it, as risks start after 20 weeks
A.why: NG133 1.3.3: stop ACE inhibitors if a woman becomes pregnant, preferably within 2 working days of notification, and offer alternatives.

whyNot.0: Waiting until 12 weeks continues exposure to a drug linked with congenital abnormalities.
whyNot.2: Her hypertension still needs treatment with an alternative medicine.
whyNot.3: NICE links ACE inhibitors with congenital abnormalities, so action is needed now.

A.q: A breastfeeding mother is going home on an antihypertensive. What should the midwife advise her to watch for in her baby?
options: Rapid weight gain and inconsolable crying
A.why: NG133 1.9.3: advise women to monitor their babies for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries or poor feeding.

whyNot.0: These are not the effects NICE highlights for antihypertensives in milk.
whyNot.1: These suggest liver problems or jaundice, not antihypertensive effects.
whyNot.2: These are not recognised antihypertensive effects in a breastfed baby.

B.q: Molly is breastfeeding and has postnatal hypertension needing treatment. She is of white British origin. Which medicine does NICE recommend first?
B.why: NG133 1.9.4: offer enalapril to treat hypertension in the postnatal period, with monitoring of maternal renal function and potassium.

whyNot.0: Losartan is an ARB, avoided where possible when breastfeeding (1.9.8).
whyNot.2: Diuretics are avoided where possible when breastfeeding (1.9.8).
whyNot.3: NICE advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days after the birth and changing treatment.

B.q: On day 2 after a caesarean, Ines is breastfeeding and asks for something stronger than paracetamol. What does SPS advise?
options: Codeine is fine for up to 3 days
Codeine is fine once baby is 2 weeks old
B.why: SPS: codeine should not be used during breastfeeding; a non-opioid analgesic such as paracetamol or ibuprofen should be used wherever possible.

whyNot.0: Codeine should not be used in breastfeeding; the 3-day point in SPS advice is about close supervision of regular opioids such as dihydrocodeine or tramadol.
whyNot.1: Stopping breastfeeding is not needed; a suitable alternative analgesic is chosen.
whyNot.3: SPS advises against codeine in breastfeeding, not a delay before using it.

B.q: A midwife needs evidence-based professional information on the fetal risk of a medicine a woman took in early pregnancy. Which source is most appropriate?
B.why: SPS: UKTIS produces evidence-based information on fetal risk from medicine and chemical exposures in pregnancy, with open-access summaries for professionals.

whyNot.0: Leaflet disclaimers often reflect lack of testing rather than evidence.
whyNot.1: Yellow Card is for reporting suspected adverse reactions, not risk assessment.
whyNot.2: The Medicines Learning Portal is a training resource, not an exposure advice service.

C.q: Jade has epilepsy, takes sodium valproate and attends booking at 7 weeks after an unplanned pregnancy. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Urgent specialist review; not stopping it herself
Advise her to stop taking the valproate from today
Continue as normal and review at the anomaly scan
Switch her to carbamazepine at the booking visit
C.why: MHRA: no one should stop valproate without specialist advice, and a woman who is pregnant should contact her doctor at once. The midwife escalates the same day (and she needs 5 mg folic acid, NG247 1.1.5).

whyNot.1: Stopping antiepileptics abruptly risks seizures; the decision is for her specialist.
whyNot.2: Delaying review to 20 weeks misses the chance to reduce ongoing exposure.
whyNot.3: Switching drugs is a specialist decision, and carbamazepine also carries malformation risk.

C.q: Abi has bipolar disorder and has continued lithium through pregnancy. She wants to breastfeed. What should she be told?
options: Lithium does not pass into breast milk
Lithium can reach high levels in breast milk
Breastfeeding lowers her lithium levels safely
Lithium is stopped at birth until 6 weeks
C.why: CG192 1.4.34: women should know that lithium levels may be high in breast milk, with a risk of toxicity for the baby, so specialist advice is needed.

whyNot.0: Lithium does pass into breast milk, sometimes at high levels.
whyNot.2: Breastfeeding does not safely lower maternal lithium; the baby is exposed.
whyNot.3: There is no NICE rule to stop lithium until 6 weeks; relapse risk is highest postnatally.

C.q: Funmi, of Black African family origin, needs treatment for postnatal hypertension and is breastfeeding. She has not taken antihypertensives before. Which medicine does NICE suggest?
C.why: NG133 1.9.5: for women of Black African or Caribbean family origin, consider nifedipine (or amlodipine if previously used successfully).

whyNot.0: ARBs such as losartan are avoided where possible when breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: Methyldopa is stopped within 2 days of the birth.
whyNot.2: Diuretics are avoided where possible when breastfeeding.

reteach.title: Before birth, avoid; after birth, adapt
reteach.question: Why can enalapril be wrong at 8 weeks of pregnancy but right on day 4 after birth?

blocks.body: In pregnancy the drug reaches the developing fetus directly through the placenta, so known teratogens are avoided and switched early. After birth, the baby receives only what passes into breast milk, usually a tiny fraction. That is why NICE stops ACE inhibitors in pregnancy but offers enalapril postnatally, and why the default is to keep breastfeeding and watch the baby.

blocks.text: A leaflet saying 'not recommended in breastfeeding' usually means 'not tested', not 'proven harmful' (NG133 1.9.2). Check UKTIS, SPS or the BNF before advising.

explain.body: NICE does not offer lithium in pregnancy unless antipsychotics have not worked, because of a risk of fetal heart malformations when taken in the first trimester; levels may also be high in breast milk (CG192 1.4.33-1.4.34).

items.label: Stop; level 12 h after last dose

test.q: In which part of pregnancy is lithium linked to fetal heart malformations?
test.why: CG192 1.4.34: there is a risk of fetal heart malformations when lithium is taken in the first trimester.

whyNot.1: The heart forms in early pregnancy, so the malformation risk is first trimester.
whyNot.2: Third-trimester concerns are about levels and toxicity, not heart formation.
whyNot.3: In labour lithium is stopped because of toxicity risk, not malformation.

explain.body: NICE asks prescribers to avoid diuretics and angiotensin receptor blockers where possible in women who are breastfeeding or expressing milk, and to prefer once-daily medicines (NG133 1.9.7-1.9.8).

test.q: Which antihypertensives should be avoided where possible in a woman who is breastfeeding?
test.why: NG133 1.9.8: where possible, avoid diuretics or angiotensin receptor blockers in the postnatal period in women who are breastfeeding or expressing milk.

whyNot.0: Enalapril and nifedipine are NICE postnatal choices.
whyNot.1: Labetalol or atenolol can be added if BP is not controlled.
whyNot.3: Amlodipine and enalapril are recommended options.

explain.h: Do not default to stopping breastfeeding
explain.body: SPS: stopping breastfeeding when a medicine is prescribed is not a no-risk option. The aim is to let the mother keep breastfeeding while taking the most appropriate treatment, and to seek expert advice before advising against it.

test.q: A colleague tells a mother to stop breastfeeding 'to be safe' while she takes a new medicine. What does SPS guidance say?
options: Most medicines reach unsafe levels in breast milk
Express and discard as a routine
test.why: SPS: advising against breastfeeding carries risk; most medicines can be used during breastfeeding, and expert advice should be sought before advising against it.

whyNot.0: Stopping breastfeeding is not a no-risk option.
whyNot.2: SPS states most medicines can be used during breastfeeding.
whyNot.3: Expressing and discarding is a specialist option for specific hazardous medicines, not routine.

explain.body: UKTIS gives professionals evidence on fetal risk; BUMPS turns it into leaflets for women; SPS and UKDILAS advise on breastfeeding; the BNF and SPC give doses and contraindications.

test.q: Which resource is designed for women themselves, giving information on medicines in pregnancy?
test.why: BUMPS (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) provides information leaflets for women, based on UKTIS scientific material.

whyNot.0: TOXBASE is a professional poisons database needing a login.
whyNot.1: The BNF is a professional prescribing reference.
whyNot.3: Detailed UKTIS monographs are written for healthcare professionals.
